categories: Articles needing additional references from November 2014

profile.name: Zonaradiko
profile.tagline: A Thracian belt-hold line dance that twists into tight spirals and fast steps
profile.insight: Named after the zonari or belt that dancers hold, this open-circle dance anchored displaced communities across Evros following the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.
profile.profile: Zonaradiko is a traditional folk dance originating from Thrace in northeastern Greece. Dancers form an open line or circle, gripping the belts of those adjacent to them. The dance is shared across the border in southeastern Bulgaria, where it is known as Pravo or Pravo Trakijsko Horo. Following the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, Zonaradiko served as a primary cultural touchstone for diverse Greek populations settling in the Evros region.
profile.profile_long:
Zonaradiko is an open-circle folk dance native to the historical region of Thrace in northeastern Greece. Its defining feature is its grip: rather than linking hands or shoulder-to-shoulder holds, dancers reach across to grip the zonaria—the cloth belts or sashes—worn around the waists of the participants on either side. Executed with bent knees throughout, the dance moves in a 12-count pattern comprising 8 basic steps, shifting between slow steady progression and rapid accelerations.

In regional practice, particularly across the northern Evros prefecture, Zonaradiko holds a prominent place in social gatherings. Following the population exchanges mandated by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, the Evros area received wave after wave of incoming groups, including indigenous Thracians, refugees from Bulgarian and Turkish Thrace, Pontic Greeks, and Cappadocians. In this multi-ethnic mosaic, Zonaradiko acted as a unifying medium of shared identification across diverse migrant backgrounds.

Across Thrace, local variations dictate the structural evolution of the line. In western Thrace, men historically lead the front of the line while women follow toward the rear. As the sequence nears its climax, the lead dancer spirals the line inward into the center, winding the circle tightly around himself before unwinding the chain back into an open circle. In northern Thrace, the steady tempo of the primary Zonaradiko frequently accelerates into a fast-paced transition known as the tsestos.

During the tsestos phase, structural divisions often occur within the performance space. Dancers either transition together into rapid tsestos footwork, or a secondary belt-hold line forms inside the original circle toward the center. Historically, men would step out to perform the intense tsestos steps in an inner ring while women either paused to watch or maintained the steady Pravo rhythm in the outer circle.

sections.origins_and_history: Zonaradiko originated in the Thrace region spanning northern Greece and neighbouring territories. Following the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, refugee populations—including Cappadocians, Pontic Greeks, and Thracians from Bulgaria and Turkey—settled heavily in northern Evros, where the dance emerged as an identity marker across these distinct groups. The movement sequence corresponds directly to the Bulgarian Pravo Trakijsko Horo.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers stand in an open circle or line with knees bent throughout the dance, holding the waist belts (zonaria) of adjacent dancers with the leader on the far right. The basic structure consists of 12 counts containing 8 steps. In western Thrace variants, the line leads into a spiral around the leader before untwisting. When accelerating into the fast tsestos phase, dancers maintain the belt-hold while forming an inner circle or maintaining a distinct inner line.
sections.music_and_instruments: Zonaradiko is danced to traditional Thracian folk melodies. Specific musical compositions cited for the dance include 'Lianohortarouthyia' (Λιανοχορταρούδια), 'Steryios Pismanipsi' (Στέργιος Πισμάνιψι), and 'Vasilkouda' (Βασιλκούδα).
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is traditionally performed in open-circle formations at village gatherings throughout Thrace. A crucial element of the attire is the zonari (cloth belt or sash) worn around the waist, which provides the handhold for the line.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed as a social village dance across Greek and Bulgarian Thrace, Zonaradiko served as a vital cultural binder for indigenous residents and resettled refugee groups in northern Evros after 1923.
sections.notable_figures: No individual historical choreographers or historical soloists are detailed in the sources.
sections.regional_variants: In northern Thrace, Zonaradiko shifts into a fast phase known as tsestos. In western Thrace, men lead the head of the line while women take the tail, executing a distinctive winding and unwinding spiral pattern toward the center of the floor. In southeastern Bulgaria, the identical step sequence is performed under the name Pravo Trakijsko Horo.
sections.lineage: Directly related to the broader Balkan family of Pravo line dances found across Bulgaria and Greece.

basic_steps: Maintain a constant bend in both knees throughout all steps.
Grasp the cloth belt (zonari) of the dancer on your left and right.
Execute the basic 8-step sequence spread over 12 counts while moving in an open circle.
When transitioning to tsestos, maintain the belt grip while accelerating footwork or stepping into an inner circle.
teaching.formation: Open circle or line holding adjacent dancers' belts (zonaria), led from the right.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners must maintain bent knees and a firm belt grip while keeping tempo with the open-circle movement.

gaps: Specific historical origin dates prior to the 20th century are not detailed in the sources.
Exact musical meter signature is not explicitly stated in the sources beyond the count structure.

claims.text: Dancers hold adjacent belts during the dance.
claims.quote: Dancers hold the adjacent dancer's zonaria (belt) during the dance.

claims.text: The dance is known as Pravo in Bulgaria.
claims.quote: The same dance is done in Bulgaria under the name Pravo.

claims.text: The dance accelerates into tsestos in northern Thrace.
claims.quote: In northern Thrace, zonaradikos turns into a fast tsestos.

claims.text: The entire dance is executed with knees bent.
claims.quote: The entire dance is done with the knees bent.

claims.text: Songs like Lianohortarouthyia are traditional zonaradika tunes.
claims.quote: Songs like Lianohortarouthyia (Λιανοχορταρούδια), Steryios Pismanipsi (Στέργιος Πισμάνιψι), and Vasilkouda (Βασιλκούδα) are all zonaradika.

claims.text: The dance consists of 12 counts and 8 basic steps in an open circle.
claims.quote: Der Zonaradikos (Ζωναράδικος) ist ein Tanz aus Thrakien, der wie fast alle griechischen Tänze im offenen Kreis getanzt wird und aus zwölf Zeiten (im Grundtanz 8 Schritten) besteht.

claims.text: In southeastern Bulgaria, the same step combination is called Pravo Trakijsko Horo.
claims.quote: Die gleiche Schrittkombination wird auch im südöstlichen Bulgarien getanzt und heißt dort Pravo Trakijsko Horo.

claims.text: It is a central dance in the northern Evros region.
claims.quote: Der Zonaradikos ist einer der wichtigsten Tänze der nördlichen Region Evros

claims.text: Refugees settled in the Evros region primarily after the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.
claims.quote: Die meisten von ihnen zogen nach dem Vertrag von Lausanne im Jahr 1923 ins Gebiet.
